samples.text:
Nowadays, in many cities people can rent electric scooters and bicycles by the hour using a phone app. Although this idea seems modern and useful, I believe it is more a negative development than a positive one.

It is true that these vehicles have some advantages. They are cheap and easy to use for short journeys, for example from the train station to the office. They also do not produce pollution like cars, so they can help to reduce traffic and make the air more cleaner.

However, the biggest problem is safety. Many riders of electric scooters go very fast and they do not wear a helmet. Some of them ride on the pavement, which is very dangerous for pedestrians, especially old people and children. In my city, I often see scooters that nearly hit people who are walking, and there has been many accidents. Also, some users do not know the traffic rules, because they only use the scooter one or two time.

Another problem is that these scooters and bikes are often left everywhere. Because users can leave them in any place, many of them block the pavement or the entrance of buildings. This is annoying for everyone and particularly difficult for people in wheelchair or with a pushchair. In some places scooters are even thrown into rivers, which make more pollution.

In conclusion, although hire scooters and bicycles are convenient and do not pollute the air, I think they are a negative development because they cause accidents and make the streets messy. The government should make strict rules, for example speed limits and special parking areas, otherwise the problems will continue.
samples.why: Clear negative position · relevant ideas supported with a personal example but some are general · linking present but repetitive · adequate vocabulary · several errors in comparatives, agreement and plurals.

samples.text:
Rentable electric scooters and bicycles, unlocked with a smartphone and paid for by the hour, have appeared on the streets of many cities in recent years. Despite some genuine problems, I believe this is a positive development for urban life.

The principal advantage is that these vehicles offer a practical alternative to cars for short trips. Many car journeys in cities cover only a few kilometres, which could easily be made by bike or scooter. Hire schemes make this option available to people who do not own a bicycle or have nowhere to store one. They are especially useful for the so-called last mile, the distance between a train station or bus stop and a person's final destination, and they can therefore encourage more people to use public transport.

Moreover, if these schemes replace even a small proportion of car journeys, the environmental benefits are significant. Fewer cars means less congestion, lower emissions and cleaner air, which improves public health. Cycling also provides exercise, and people who try a hire bike may decide to cycle more regularly.

Of course, the schemes have caused problems. Scooters are sometimes ridden dangerously on pavements, and vehicles are frequently left lying in the middle of footpaths, creating obstacles for pedestrians, particularly those with poor eyesight or limited mobility. However, these are problems of management rather than reasons to reject the idea. Cities can introduce designated parking zones, speed limits and fines for irresponsible users, as some have already done successfully.

In conclusion, although shared scooters and bicycles require careful regulation, they provide a cheap, flexible and environmentally friendly way of getting around cities. For these reasons, I consider their growing popularity to be a positive trend.
samples.why: Clear positive position throughout · ideas extended with specific support (last mile, congestion) · problems addressed logically · good range of linking · some less common vocabulary · mostly error-free.

samples.text:
Dockless electric scooters and hire bicycles, located and unlocked through a smartphone, have become a familiar sight in many cities. Their arrival has provoked strong reactions, from enthusiasm about greener transport to irritation at cluttered pavements. Weighing these responses, I consider the trend a positive one, albeit one that demands firm regulation.

The strongest argument in their favour concerns the way people move through cities. A striking number of urban car journeys are short enough to be walked or cycled, yet habit and convenience keep drivers behind the wheel. Hire schemes lower the barriers to change: users need not buy, maintain or store a vehicle, and they can make a one-way trip without worrying about returning it. Crucially, scooters and bikes bridge the gap between public transport stops and people's homes or workplaces, making trains and buses a realistic option for those who previously found them impractical.

The potential environmental and social returns are considerable. Every car journey replaced reduces congestion and emissions, and cleaner streets benefit everyone, not only those who ride. For residents who cannot afford a car, affordable short-term hire also widens access to jobs and services across the city.

The drawbacks, nonetheless, are real and visible. Poorly parked scooters obstruct pavements, posing a particular hazard to blind and elderly pedestrians, and reckless riding has led to injuries. Yet these problems stem from the way schemes were initially introduced, often with minimal oversight, rather than from the vehicles themselves. Cities that have imposed designated parking bays, speed restrictions in pedestrian areas and penalties for operators have largely brought them under control.

In conclusion, shared scooters and bicycles offer a flexible, low-carbon complement to public transport. Provided that authorities regulate them rigorously, their spread should be welcomed as a positive development.
samples.why: Clear, well-qualified positive judgement · ideas logically sequenced and fully extended · drawbacks weighed rather than listed · natural, precise vocabulary · wide range of structures with full control.
